explanation: Greedy decoding is meant to be deterministic, but parallel numeric operations and batching can alter tiny values and flip close choices. Providers may also update serving. Do not rely on bit-identical output.

text: Why does TTFT usually grow when the prompt gets longer?
options: The model must process the whole prompt (prefill) before it can produce the first output token
Longer prompts make the model faster, because it has more material to work with and warms up on the extra text
The first token is always the longest word of the reply
The network cables slow down whenever more data passes through them
explanation: Prefill computes the prompt's internal states before generation starts, so more input tokens mean more work before the first token. Prompt caching or shorter prompts can reduce it.

text: A mobile app must work without internet and sync later. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Show an error message whenever the device is offline and block every action until the connection comes back
Store everything only on the server and require a connection at all times
Write to a local database first, queue changes, sync when online and define conflict rules
Ask users to retype their data later, once the connection is back
explanation: A local-first design keeps the app usable offline. Syncing needs an explicit strategy for retries and conflicts, such as last-write-wins or merge rules, depending on the data.

text: You must remove a field from a public API that thousands of apps use. What is the safest approach?
options: Rename the field silently and hope that no client is using the old name
Delete it on Friday night, when the fewest users are online
Introduce a new version or deprecate with a timeline, and keep the old behaviour until clients migrate
Return an empty string instead, so that clients do not crash right away
explanation: Breaking changes should be versioned or phased with clear deprecation notices. Adding fields is usually safe; removing or changing meaning is not.

text: Why is adding an index on every column of a table a poor idea?
options: Indexes can only be created once per database, so every extra one that you add would simply be wasted effort
Indexes make the stored data unreadable for the application
Databases forbid more than one index per table for safety
Each index uses storage and slows writes, so indexes should follow actual query patterns
explanation: Every insert or update must also maintain every index. Index the columns used in frequent filters, joins and sorts, and verify with the query plan.

text: A very popular cached key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. What is this called and how can it be reduced?
options: A cache hit, which is solved by adding many more keys to the cache
A schema migration, which is solved by restarting the whole database
A deadlock, which is solved by deleting the entire cache
A cache stampede; use request coalescing or locking, jittered TTLs or serving stale data while refreshing
explanation: When many callers miss simultaneously they all recompute the value. Let one caller rebuild it while others wait or get slightly stale data, and randomise TTLs so hot keys do not expire together.

text: Users keep getting logged out after you add a second app server because sessions are kept in each server's memory. What is the proper fix?
options: Move sessions to a shared store (or use signed tokens) so any server can serve any request
Tell the users to refresh the page again and again whenever they find that they have been logged out of the app
Remove the second server again, since it is the cause of the problem
Disable logins completely until the traffic has gone down
explanation: Stateless application servers keep user state outside the process. Sticky sessions are a stopgap that complicates failover and scaling.

text: What triggered Linus Torvalds to create Git in 2005?
options: The Linux kernel lost access to its proprietary version-control tool and needed a fast, distributed replacement
A university assignment that Torvalds had to finish for a computer science course
Microsoft asked him to replace SVN with a faster internal tool that the company wanted to use for Windows development
Linux had no way at all of storing files, so a tool was urgently required
explanation: After the licence arrangement for the tool used by Linux kernel developers ended, Torvalds wrote Git within weeks, prioritising speed, distributed work and data integrity through content hashes.

text: In Unicode, the character 'é' can be one code point or 'e' plus a combining accent. Why does this matter to programmers?
options: Two visually identical strings can compare as different unless you normalise them
It never matters, because every program and every database shows and compares the two forms in exactly the same way
Only fonts care about the difference, never the program logic
It makes UTF-8 invalid, so such text can never be stored safely
explanation: Both forms render the same but have different code points, so equality, search and hashing can fail. Normalise (for example to NFC) before comparing user text. The same issue affects Arabic letter forms and diacritics.

text: A Kotlin app consumes JSON with snake_case fields. What is the cleanest way to keep idiomatic camelCase in the code?
options: Rename every Kotlin property to snake_case so that it matches the JSON exactly
Configure or annotate the serializer to map field names at the boundary
Ask the server team to change nothing and simply ignore the code style
Parse the JSON manually in every single place where it is needed
explanation: Mapping at the boundary keeps each side idiomatic and localises the convention difference in one place, such as a naming strategy or serial-name annotations.

text: 'It works on my machine' but fails on a teammate's. What is the most durable fix?
options: Ship the developer's laptop to the teammate so that both have the same machine
Tell the teammate to try again later and hope that the problem has gone
Add much more logging to the code and wait to see what appears
Make the environment reproducible with pinned dependencies and a container or lockfile
explanation: Differences in versions, configuration and OS cause such failures. Pinning dependencies and defining the environment as code makes builds repeatable for everyone and in CI.

text: In language modelling, what does a lower perplexity indicate?
options: The model assigns higher probability to the real text, so it is less 'surprised' by it
The language model is larger, with many more parameters and a much longer training time than the other models
The language model is slower at generating every token of its answer
The text that was tested is written in Arabic rather than in English
explanation: Perplexity comes from information theory (entropy) and measures how well a model predicts a sample. It is useful for comparing models on the same data and tokenizer, but does not alone prove usefulness.

text: Why can byte-level BPE encode any string, even emoji or unseen scripts, without an 'unknown' token?
options: It translates every text to English first and then encodes the English version, so the original text is never used
It stores every sentence that has ever been written in a huge lookup table
Its base vocabulary contains every possible byte, so any text can at least be spelled out
It simply ignores any unknown characters instead of encoding them
explanation: Starting from 256 byte values guarantees coverage of any UTF-8 text. Rare scripts simply become longer sequences of byte-level pieces, which is another reason they cost more tokens.

text: A service sends 50,000 requests a day with 1,000 English input tokens each, at $2 per 1M input tokens. If the Arabic version needs 1.6× the tokens, what is the extra daily input cost?
explanation: English: 50M tokens × $2/M = $100. Arabic: 80M tokens = $160. The difference is $60 per day. The 1.6 ratio is an assumption: measure the real one for your texts and model.

text: Why can a trailing space at the end of a completion-style prompt hurt the output?
options: Spaces are charged at double the price of other characters, which quickly adds to the cost of every single prompt you send
Tokenizers usually attach the space to the next word, so the prompt ends in an unnatural split the model rarely saw
The model cannot read spaces at all and is confused by them
Trailing spaces delete the whole prompt before it reaches the model
explanation: In typical vocabularies the space belongs to the following word-token. A prompt ending in a lone space forces an unusual boundary, which can change what the model predicts next.

text: To compare how efficiently tokenizers handle different languages fairly, which measurement is most meaningful?
options: Tokens per word in each language, counted separately for every text
Tokens needed for parallel texts with the same meaning
The size of the vocabulary file that each tokenizer ships with
Characters per second that each model is able to produce
explanation: Words are defined differently across languages, so tokens-per-word misleads. Using aligned translations and comparing token counts for the same content gives a fairer ratio.

text: Your app needs machine-readable output. Which is the strongest approach where the API supports it?
options: Ask politely for JSON in the prompt only, and hope that the model complies with the format every single time
Use the API's structured-output or schema-constrained mode, and still validate in code
Parse the free text with regular expressions only, without any schema
Ask the user to copy the output into the right fields manually
explanation: Constrained or schema-guided generation greatly reduces malformed output, but validation and error handling remain necessary because values can still be wrong.

text: Which investment most improves an AI coding agent's results across many tasks in your repository?
options: Removing all of the tests, so that the agent is never blocked by a failure and can finish every task it starts
A longer and more random prompt written from scratch for each task
Clear build and test commands, documented conventions and a reliable test suite
Hiding the layout of the code so that the agent cannot get confused
explanation: Agents work best when they can verify their changes. Documented commands and conventions plus fast, trustworthy tests give feedback to iterate against; small, well-scoped tasks help too.

text: What supply-chain risk arises when an AI assistant suggests a package name that does not exist?
options: None at all, because the package manager automatically blocks unknown names and refuses to install anything suspicious or invented
The package would simply be faster than the real one
The assistant will pay for the package if it turns out to be harmful
An attacker can publish a malicious package under that invented name and wait for developers to install it
explanation: Hallucinated dependency names can be registered by attackers. Verify that a package exists, is maintained and is the intended one before installing, and review install scripts.

text: What is the purpose of content-provenance standards such as C2PA 'Content Credentials' for AI images?
options: They make images load faster by compressing them in the background
They attach verifiable metadata about origin and edits, though it can be stripped
They guarantee that the image shows something that really happened, and prove that nobody has edited it afterwards
They compress the colours of the image to save storage space
explanation: Provenance metadata records how content was created or edited and by which tool. It helps trust but is not proof of truth, and metadata can be removed when images are re-saved or screenshotted.

text: You build an AI invoice extractor. Which evaluation is most convincing before deployment?
options: A live demo on one single clean invoice that was chosen by the developer
The model's own statement that its extraction is accurate and reliable, when it is asked directly after the test
Field-level accuracy against a labelled set of real, messy invoices
The number of pages that the system processes per minute
explanation: Real documents vary in layout and quality. Per-field accuracy on a labelled representative set shows where extraction fails and tracks improvement. Speed does not show correctness.

text: An AI search tool often cites low-quality SEO pages. What is a sound mitigation?
options: Disable all sources, so that the tool no longer shows any low-quality pages and only answers from its own memory
Trust the first link, since search engines put the best result first
Ask for many more links without actually reading any of them
Prefer or restrict sources to authoritative domains and open the primary source before relying on it
explanation: Retrieval quality depends on what the index and ranking surface. Prioritising official or primary sources and reading them yourself reduces reliance on weak pages.

text: A support bot must answer from a 2,000-page handbook that changes monthly. Which approach is generally most maintainable?
options: Fine-tune a brand-new model after every single edit to the handbook
Retrieve relevant passages at query time from an index that you refresh when the handbook changes
Paste the whole 2,000-page handbook into every single prompt
Disable all updates so that the handbook never has to change
explanation: Retrieval separates knowledge from model weights: updating means re-indexing, not retraining. It also lets you cite passages. Fine-tuning is better for style or behaviour than for frequently changing facts.

text: For a very long prompt with one critical constraint, which structure best guards against it being overlooked?
options: State it near the start and restate it briefly at the end, after the long material
Never state the constraint at all, since a good model should be able to guess it from the surrounding material
Place it only in the middle, between the long pieces of material
Write it in tiny words so that it does not take up the space
explanation: Edges are used more reliably in long contexts, so stating key instructions at the start and restating them after the documents is a cheap safeguard. Verify with tests rather than assuming.

text: An LLM router adds its own model call before every request. What trade-off must you evaluate?
options: The router's added latency and cost versus the savings from sending requests to cheaper models
Whether routers are actually able to read and understand the requests that they are sending on to the models
How many colours the logo of the routing service has
Whether routing changes the alphabet used in the final answer
explanation: Routing only helps if router overhead is small relative to savings and its mistakes are rare. Cheap rules, small classifiers or embeddings can serve as routers.

text: How does speculative decoding speed up generation?
options: A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model verifies them in one parallel step
It shortens the user's prompt so that there is less to process at first, and then restores the removed words
It deletes the difficult tokens from the answer before showing it
It skips the large model entirely and only ever uses the small one
explanation: When the draft is mostly right, several tokens are accepted per large-model step. Verification keeps the output distribution of the large model, so quality is preserved while latency falls.

text: For a latency promise to users, why are p95 or p99 values more informative than the average TTFT?
options: Averages are always larger than the percentile values, so they overstate the delay that the users really feel
Averages cannot be calculated for latency measurements at all
Percentiles are much cheaper to compute than a simple average
Averages hide slow outliers that real users still experience
explanation: A few very slow requests barely move the mean but ruin the experience for some users. Percentiles describe the tail, which is what service-level targets usually need.

text: In clean or hexagonal architecture, what does the dependency rule state?
options: Domain code should depend directly on the UI framework that is being used, so that screens and rules stay perfectly in sync
All layers must depend on the database, since it is the source of truth
Dependencies between the layers should be circular so that they stay in sync
Source dependencies point inward: business rules do not depend on frameworks, UI or storage details
explanation: Keeping business logic independent of frameworks and I/O makes it testable and easier to change technologies. Outer layers adapt to the domain, not the other way around.

text: What does the strangler fig pattern describe when migrating from a legacy monolith?
options: Deleting the old system in one single night and launching the new one in its place, with no gradual migration at all
Duplicating the database forever so that both systems stay in sync
Gradually routing functionality to new services or modules until the old system can be retired
Rewriting everything privately for years before showing it to anyone
explanation: Incremental replacement reduces risk: a facade routes some requests to new code while the rest still goes to the old system, with the old parts removed over time.

text: A GraphQL query for 50 posts triggers 51 database queries (one for posts plus one per author). What is this problem and a common fix?
options: The N+1 query problem; batch loads with a data-loader or use joins
A cache hit, which is solved by increasing the TTL of every entry in the cache and adding some more memory
A syntax error, which is solved by renaming the fields in the query
A deadlock, which is solved by restarting the whole server
explanation: Resolvers that fetch related data one item at a time multiply queries. Batching and caching per request, or fetching with joins, reduces them to a few queries.

text: In PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED level, a transaction reads a row twice and sees different values because another transaction committed in between. What is this called?
options: A cache stampede, where many requests hit the database after an expiry
A syntax error, caused by writing the query in the wrong order
A foreign key violation, caused by deleting a row that is still referenced
A non-repeatable read
explanation: READ COMMITTED sees data committed before each statement, so repeated reads can differ. REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE give stronger guarantees but require handling serialization failures with retries.

text: A service has 10 million daily active users, each making 5 requests per day. Assuming peak traffic is about 3× the average, roughly what peak requests per second must it handle?
options: About 58
About 580
About 1,750
About 17,500
explanation: Total: 50 million requests/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 580 average per second; × 3 ≈ 1,740 at peak. Back-of-envelope estimates show the order of magnitude, which guides design; the peak factor is an assumption.

text: Which 1960s language introduced classes and objects, influencing later languages such as C++ and Java?
options: COBOL
BASIC
Simula
Assembly
explanation: Simula, created in Norway for simulation, introduced classes, objects and inheritance. Smalltalk later developed the ideas into a full object-oriented environment.

text: What is the 'Year 2038 problem'?
options: Systems storing Unix time in a signed 32-bit integer overflow in January 2038
Dates before the year 2000 cannot be stored by any modern system
Computers permanently stop working at some point in 2038 because their clocks cannot count any further than that
All websites expire in 2038 because their certificates run out
explanation: Unix time counts seconds since 1970. A signed 32-bit counter reaches its maximum on 19 January 2038 and wraps negative. Using 64-bit time values removes the problem for practical purposes.

text: What was the key change when Node.js appeared in 2009?
options: JavaScript lost its event loop, so that for the first time it could finally run many tasks in parallel on servers
JavaScript became compiled into Java bytecode and ran on the JVM
Browsers were removed from the web, so scripts moved to servers
JavaScript could run outside the browser, on servers, using the V8 engine and non-blocking I/O
explanation: Node.js packaged Google's V8 engine with an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model, letting developers use JavaScript for backend services and tooling, which fuelled the npm ecosystem.

text: You test 1,000 unrelated random features for correlation with sales using a 5% significance threshold. About how many will look 'significant' purely by chance?
options: About 5
About 500
About 50
None
explanation: With a 5% false-positive rate, 1,000 tests yield about 50 chance 'discoveries'. This multiple-comparisons problem is why mining needs validation on fresh data and corrections for many tests.

text: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 1,000 commits. About how many test runs does `git bisect` need to find the guilty commit?
options: About 500
About 100
About 10
About 50
explanation: Bisect halves the search range each step, so about log2(1,000) ≈ 10 tests. It needs a reliable pass/fail check, which is another reason to write a failing test first.

text: Why can't you feed token IDs produced by one model's tokenizer into a different model?
options: The same ID maps to different text in a different vocabulary, and each model's embeddings are tied to its own vocabulary
Models only accept letters as input and cannot read numeric IDs at all
The IDs are encrypted by the tokenizer, so other models cannot decode them
IDs expire after one day, so they are useless for a different request
explanation: A token ID is an index into a specific vocabulary and embedding table. Another model interprets the number as a different piece of text. Always tokenize with the model's own tokenizer.

text: An API reply stops mid-sentence and reports finish reason 'length'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model got bored of the topic and decided to stop writing
The maximum output-token limit was reached
The prompt was too polite, so the model treated it as finished
The tokenizer failed while the answer was being generated
explanation: A 'length' finish means generation hit the configured or model maximum output tokens. Raise the limit (within the window), request a shorter answer or continue the generation.

text: Is lowercasing all user input before sending it always a safe way to save tokens?
options: Yes, because the meaning of a sentence never changes with letter case
No, because models can only read capital letters and ignore the rest
Yes, and it always cuts the token count down to about half
No, it can change meaning (names, acronyms, code) and may not reduce tokens
explanation: Case carries information, such as 'US' vs 'us' or case-sensitive identifiers. Lowercasing may also split words differently, so test the effect on both quality and token counts.

text: To save tokens, a team proposes translating every Arabic prompt to English before calling the model. What should they weigh?
options: Nothing at all, because translating first is always the better choice
Translation is free and perfect, so there is no cost or risk to weigh
Possible token savings versus translation errors, lost nuance, extra latency and cost, and the need to translate replies back
Only the colour of the interface where the translated prompts are shown
explanation: A pipeline of translate, answer, translate back adds steps and can distort meaning, especially for dialect, names and domain terms. Evaluate quality and total cost on real data before adopting it.

text: All five few-shot examples in your sentiment prompt are labelled 'positive'. What risk does this create?
options: None, because few-shot examples are simply ignored by the model
The model will refuse to answer any sentence that sounds negative
The prompt becomes illegal because it is unbalanced
The model may be biased toward answering 'positive'
explanation: Few-shot examples act as a strong signal. Unbalanced labels or a fixed order can skew predictions, so include balanced, varied examples and test with realistic inputs.

text: Which kind of flaw deserves the most attention when reviewing an AI-generated diff?
options: Slightly different colours that the editor uses to display the names of the variables inside the changed lines of code
The number of blank lines that were added between the functions
Plausible-looking code with subtle logic or security gaps, such as a missing authorisation check
Whether the comments in the code use polite and friendly words
explanation: AI output is usually fluent and well formatted, which can hide wrong assumptions. Reviewers should test edge cases and check access control, input validation and error handling explicitly.

text: Why should you never put secrets (API keys, private rules) in a chatbot's system prompt?
options: Secrets make the prompts longer than the maximum length that the model provider allows for a system prompt
Users can often extract system-prompt content through clever prompting
System prompts are public by law, so anyone may read them anyway
Models automatically delete any secrets they find in a prompt
explanation: System prompts are not a secure vault. Keep secrets on the server side, use authentication and permissions in code, and assume prompt text may leak.

text: Why should teams test an image generator with varied prompts for stereotypes before using it in a product?
options: Training data can contain biases that show up in generated people, jobs or cultures
Tests make the generated images smaller in size, so that they load faster once they are shown inside the product
Stereotypes only ever appear in written text and never in pictures
Image generators never use any real data, so they cannot be biased
explanation: Models reflect patterns in their data. Systematic checks across different roles, regions and genders help find skewed outputs so you can adjust prompts, tools or review processes.

text: To show users where an AI answer came from, which metadata should be stored with each indexed chunk?
options: The document ID, page number and character offsets
Only the font that the chunk was written in, to restore its look
Only a random number that has no connection to the source
The password of the user who uploaded the document
explanation: Source identifiers and locations allow links or highlights back to the original passage, supporting verification and corrections when the document changes.

text: When can keyword search (such as BM25) beat embedding-based semantic search?
options: Never, because semantic search is better in every possible situation
When the queries are vague opinions without any concrete keywords
When the documents are empty and contain nothing to be searched
When queries contain exact identifiers such as error codes, SKUs or function names
explanation: Embeddings capture meaning but can blur exact strings; keyword matching is precise for rare identifiers. Many systems use hybrid search combining both and then re-rank.

text: A long-running assistant must remember user facts without sending the whole chat each time. Which design is most sensible?
options: Send the entire chat history with every single request, for ever and ever, regardless of how long it has become
Store the memory only in the very first word of each new prompt
Delete the whole memory after every single message to save space
Keep recent turns, a rolling summary and retrievable stored facts
explanation: A mix of recent messages, summaries and retrieved facts bounds token use while preserving important context. Memory should be inspectable and deletable by the user.

text: A RAG system retrieves 50 passages. What does re-ranking to the best 5 mainly improve?
options: The size of the vocabulary that the tokenizer is able to use
The colour and the font in which the final answer is displayed
Precision: fewer distractors and less irrelevant text in the prompt
The number of users who are able to use the system at once
explanation: A stronger (often cross-encoder) re-ranker scores candidates more carefully than the first-stage retriever. A smaller, cleaner context lowers cost and reduces misleading or buried evidence.

text: An LLM gateway may forward your requests to several providers. What should you check before sending sensitive data?
options: The speed of the animation that plays when the logo of the gateway loads
Each provider's data-retention and training policies and any controls on provider selection
The number of different models that are listed on the gateway's website
Whether the gateway supports emoji characters in the prompts
explanation: Routing means your data can reach third parties with different terms. Confirm retention, logging and training policies and use controls that limit providers when compliance requires it.

text: Increasing the batch size on an inference server usually has what effect?
options: Higher throughput overall, but possibly higher latency for each individual request
No effect at all
Lower throughput and lower latency
Always faster for every user
explanation: Batching keeps hardware busy and processes more tokens per second in total, but requests may wait to be grouped and share compute. Tune for your latency and cost targets.

text: The first request after a quiet period has a TTFT of 12 seconds, while later requests take under 1 second. What is a likely cause?
options: A cold start: the model or server instance had to load or spin up
The model forgot how to speak English while it was waiting
The user typed too slowly while writing the first request
The tokenizer was upgraded in the middle of the sentence
explanation: Serverless or scaled-to-zero deployments may need to load weights or start containers on the first request. Mitigations include keep-warm instances, minimum replicas and warm-up requests.

text: In a Compose or React style UI, what does 'unidirectional data flow' mean?
options: State flows down to the UI and events flow up to update a single source of truth
Data only ever moves sideways between the screens of the application
The UI edits the database directly, without any other layer in between, and every screen talks to storage on its own
Every widget keeps its own private copy of the data it needs
explanation: A single source of truth with state going down and events going up makes UI behaviour predictable and testable. In Android this is commonly implemented with a ViewModel exposing StateFlow.

text: Which caching pattern writes to both the cache and the database as part of the same write operation to keep reads fresh, at the cost of slower writes?
options: Cache-aside only
Write-through
Write-around
Read-through only
explanation: Write-through updates the cache synchronously with the store, so subsequent reads see fresh data but each write pays extra latency. Cache-aside loads on demand and invalidates or updates on change.

text: A rate limiter runs INCR and then, in a separate command, EXPIRE. Why is this risky?
options: INCR cannot be used on numbers, so the counter never actually increases
EXPIRE deletes the entire database when it is called after INCR
If the process fails between the commands the key may never expire; use an atomic script or a command that sets both
Redis forbids sending two commands one after the other in a script
explanation: Two separate steps are not atomic. A crash or error in between leaves a counter without TTL, blocking users forever. Use atomic operations such as SET with EX, a Lua script or a transaction.

text: You add read replicas to scale database reads. Which new issue can appear?
options: Writes become impossible, since all of the traffic goes to the replicas
The replicas delete the data that they are not asked to read
Replication lag: a user may not immediately see data they just wrote
Queries stop using SQL as soon as a replica is added
explanation: Replicas apply changes asynchronously, so reads may be slightly behind. Route read-your-own-writes cases to the primary or use session-level consistency strategies.

text: A read-heavy feed page joins six tables and is slow. Which option can help, and what is its cost?
options: A precomputed denormalised table or materialised view; it costs extra storage and possible staleness
Delete some of the tables so that the query has fewer tables to join
Remove all of the indexes, so that the database has less to maintain
Add small random delays so that the requests do not collide
explanation: Precomputing the joined result trades storage and freshness for fast reads. Refresh it on a schedule or on change, and check the query plan and indexes before denormalising.

text: Turing's 1936 result on the halting problem has a practical consequence for tools that analyse code. Which one?
options: No analyser can perfectly decide every behaviour of every program, so tools accept false positives or negatives
Compilers must always be slower than interpreters, whatever the program is
Programs can never be tested, so every bug has to be found by reading
All loops must be removed from the code before it can be analysed
explanation: There is no general algorithm that decides whether any program halts, and by extension many non-trivial properties are undecidable in general. Practical linters and verifiers trade completeness, soundness and speed.

text: Even with a huge hash space, hash tables still need collision handling. Which idea explains why collisions appear sooner than intuition suggests?
options: The pigeonhole principle, which only applies to very small hash tables
Hash functions delete data when two keys land in the same bucket
Computers cannot count high enough to keep the keys apart
The birthday paradox: collisions become likely after roughly the square root of the space size
explanation: With N possible hash values, collisions become likely after about √N items, not N. That is why robust tables chain or probe on collisions and why cryptographic hashes need long outputs.

text: In JavaScript, why does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` run fn after the current synchronous code finishes?
options: JavaScript pauses all of the other code for a whole second before running it
Zero means never, so the callback is silently thrown away
The callback is placed in a task queue and runs only when the call stack is empty
Timers run on a separate thread that edits the variables while the code is running
explanation: JavaScript runs one call stack; timers hand their callbacks to the event loop, which executes them after the current code completes. Even a 0 ms delay does not interrupt running code.

text: How are 'scaling laws' in LLM research best described?
options: Laws of physics that have been proven by mathematics for every model
Government regulations that limit the size that a model is allowed to have
Guarantees that a bigger model will always be better at every task
Empirical regularities showing how loss tends to improve predictably with compute, data and parameters
explanation: Despite the word 'law', these are fitted trends from experiments. They guide planning but can change with architecture, data quality and evaluation, and do not guarantee gains on every task.

text: After a redesign, a site's overall conversion rate rose, yet it fell in both the mobile and desktop segments. Which explanation fits?
options: The calculation must be impossible, so the data has to contain a mistake
Conversion rates cannot change after a redesign, so it is only noise
Simpson's paradox: the traffic mix shifted toward a higher-converting segment
The data is automatically wrong whenever segments disagree with the total
explanation: Aggregates can reverse when groups of different sizes and rates change proportion. Always inspect segments and confounders before concluding that a change worked or failed.

text: What is a 'glitch token'?
options: A token that is billed at double the price of all of the other tokens
A token that is always exactly one character long, whatever the text is
A token that is used for punctuation marks only, and never for words
A vocabulary entry that was rarely or never seen in training, so its embedding is poorly learned and can cause odd behaviour
explanation: If a string earned a vocabulary slot (for example from the tokenizer's data) but barely appears in model training, the model may handle it unpredictably. It is an artefact of separate tokenizer and model training.

text: A chatbot has a 500-token system prompt. Each turn adds a 150-token user message and a 250-token reply, and the full history is resent each time. Across 8 turns, how many input tokens are billed in total?
explanation: Request k sends 500 + 150 + 400×(k−1) tokens. Summing for k = 1..8: 8×650 + 400×28 = 5,200 + 11,200 = 16,400. Ignoring the resent history (5,200) badly underestimates cost; trim or summarise history.

text: Why do language models often fail at tasks like counting the letter 'r' in a word?
options: They cannot count numbers at all, so every counting task will fail
They only read capital letters and treat lowercase letters as noise
The letters of a word are encrypted before the model sees them
They see sub-word tokens rather than individual letters
explanation: A word may be one or two tokens, so letter-level structure is not directly visible to the model. Spelling out the word letter by letter, or using code, helps.

text: For Arabic retrieval systems, why do engineers often normalise text (for example alef variants, diacritics, tatweel) before indexing?
options: So spelling variants of the same word match, while the original text is kept for display
To change the meaning of the words so that they match the query better
To reduce the file size of the index and nothing more than that
To make the text less readable, so that only the index can use it
explanation: Arabic has orthographic variants that users type inconsistently. Normalising for search and matching improves recall, but aggressive normalisation can merge distinct words, so test it and keep the original for display.

text: You use an LLM as a judge to compare two prompt versions. Which known bias should you control for?
options: Position and verbosity bias: judges may favour the first answer or longer answers
Colour bias, where judges prefer answers that are shown in a certain colour
Alphabet bias, where judges prefer answers that start with early letters
None at all, because judges are neutral and never favour any answer
explanation: LLM judges can be swayed by order and length. Randomise or swap positions, use clear rubrics, and spot-check with human review, especially for decisions that matter.

text: You let an AI agent run shell commands in your project. Which setup is safest?
options: Give it your production credentials so that it can test the commands for real
Run it as an administrator on your main machine, with no review of its commands
Disable version control so that it cannot change the history of the project
Use a sandbox or container with least privilege, no production secrets and review of risky commands
explanation: Agents can execute harmful commands through error or injected instructions. Isolation, minimal permissions, approvals for destructive actions and version control limit the damage.

text: What reduces factual hallucinations more reliably than only lowering the temperature?
options: Adding more exclamation marks to the prompt so that it sounds more certain
Grounding the answer in retrieved sources, requiring citations and allowing the model to say it does not know
Asking for a much longer answer so that the model has more room to be right
Using a slower internet connection so the model has time to think
explanation: Low temperature reduces randomness but does not give the model facts. Retrieval plus a permitted 'unknown' answer and source checks address the actual cause: lack of grounded information.

text: You need a consistent set of crisp, scalable UI icons. Which approach is generally best?
options: Use a vector icon set or design tool, optionally with AI for ideas
Generate each icon with a raster image generator and trust the style to match
Take screenshots
Draw them in a text editor
explanation: UI icons need exact geometry, consistent stroke and clean scaling, which vector tools provide. Raster generators vary between outputs and give pixel images that blur when scaled.

text: You process scanned Arabic documents with OCR. Which practice most improves reliability?
options: Assume that OCR is already perfect for Arabic, so no testing is needed
Choose an engine with Arabic support, test it on representative scans and verify mixed text, numbers and reading order
Ignore the numbers on the page, since they are rarely important
Convert the whole text to lowercase letters before reading it
explanation: Arabic OCR must handle connected letters, diacritics, right-to-left order and embedded Latin text or numerals. Measuring error rates on your own scans shows whether post-processing or manual review is needed.

text: A research agent returns a 20-page report with 60 citations. What is an efficient quality check?
options: Open a sample of the citations, focusing on the claims that matter most, and check that the pages really support them
Count how many citations the report contains, and accept it if it is many
Trust the report because it is long and looks thorough and professional
Ask the agent whether it is sure, and accept whatever it answers
explanation: Length and citation count do not prove accuracy. Verifying high-impact claims and a random sample estimates reliability; asking the same system to confirm itself is weak evidence.

text: A hypothetical model charges $3 per 1M input tokens. An app sends 120,000-token prompts 10,000 times a day, while a retrieval design would send 6,000 tokens. What is the approximate daily input saving?
explanation: Long prompts: 120,000 × 10,000 = 1.2B tokens → $3,600. Retrieval: 6,000 × 10,000 = 60M tokens → $180. Saving ≈ $3,420 per day, before comparing quality and any retrieval infrastructure cost. Prices here are illustrative.

text: A model scores perfectly on a single-fact 'needle in a haystack' test, yet fails on your task that requires combining many facts across a long document. Why?
options: The test is always wrong, so its score should be ignored in every case
Finding one planted fact is easier than aggregating or reasoning over many dispersed facts
Long documents never contain any facts that could be found or combined
The model changes its mind overnight, so its answers cannot be compared
explanation: Synthetic retrieval tests measure a narrow ability. Tasks needing multi-hop reasoning, counting or summarising across the text stress the model differently, so evaluate on tasks that resemble yours.

text: You plan to switch your app to a newer model version. Which rollout is most responsible?
options: Switch all of the users at once without running any tests beforehand
Trust the release notes alone, since the provider has already tested everything
Run your regression set and shadow or canary traffic, compare quality, cost and latency, then roll out gradually with a rollback path
Switch only on Fridays, so that any problems are found over the weekend
explanation: Model versions change style, safety behaviour and cost. Offline evaluation, limited exposure and the ability to roll back catch regressions before most users are affected.

text: What is the main idea of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model?
options: For each token only a few expert sub-networks are activated, lowering compute per token compared with a dense model of the same total size
It uses one single expert for all of the tokens, which makes it very small
It mixes two human languages inside every one of its layers
It needs no memory at all, since the experts are loaded only when needed
explanation: A router selects a few experts per token, so active parameters are fewer than total parameters. Compute per token drops, but memory to hold all experts and routing complexity remain.

text: An assistant calls a search tool before answering. Why is plain 'time to first token' misleading for user experience?
options: The first visible text of the final answer may arrive only after tool latency, so you should trace each stage and the time to first useful text
Streaming is impossible whenever a model is allowed to use tools
Users read tokens backwards, starting from the end of the answer
Tools do not exist in real applications, so the metric is simply unused
explanation: In agentic flows the model may think, call tools and then answer. Per-stage tracing (model start, tool time, final answer start) shows where users actually wait.

text: A service saves an order to its database and then publishes an 'order created' event. If it crashes between the two steps, events are lost. Which pattern addresses this?
options: Ignore the lost event, since the next order will trigger a similar one
Retry the whole request manually each time that a crash is noticed
The transactional outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and publish it from there
Delete the order, so that the database and the events stay consistent
explanation: A dual write to two systems cannot be atomic. The outbox stores the event with the data in one transaction, and a relay publishes it at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates (be idempotent).

text: Several microservices read and write the same database tables directly. What is the main problem?
options: They are tightly coupled through the shared schema, so a change in one can break the others and independent deployment is lost
The tables become too colourful, which makes them hard to read in tools
Databases cannot be shared between services under any circumstances
The services automatically become faster because they share the same data
explanation: A common guideline is that each service owns its data and exposes it through an API or events. A shared schema recreates a distributed monolith with the costs of both styles.

text: Your API is being overloaded by a client that retries instantly after errors. Which combination is best practice?
options: Return HTTP 200 for everything, so that the clients never see any error
Ban all of the clients permanently until the overload stops
Rate-limit with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header, and have clients back off exponentially with jitter
Increase the timeout to one hour so that clients wait quietly
explanation: Rate limits protect shared capacity, 429 tells clients to slow down, and exponential backoff with random jitter avoids synchronised retry storms.

text: Transaction A locks row 1 then wants row 2; transaction B locks row 2 then wants row 1. PostgreSQL aborts one of them. What is this and how do you reduce it?
options: A cache miss, which is reduced by adding more RAM to the database server
A syntax error, which is reduced by rewriting the SQL of both transactions
A deadlock; acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short and retry the aborted one
Replication lag, which is reduced by adding more read replicas
explanation: Opposite lock orders create a cycle. PostgreSQL detects it and cancels one transaction, so the application must be ready to retry. Consistent ordering and short transactions make deadlocks rarer.

text: A Redis instance restarts and all cached sessions vanish, logging users out. What does this reveal?
options: Sessions can never be stored in Redis, so a different tool must always be used
Redis is broken and has to be replaced with a more reliable database
By default Redis keeps data in memory; you need persistence or replication if the data must survive, or a design where it can be rebuilt
Users must change their passwords every time that the server restarts
explanation: Redis offers snapshots (RDB) and append-only logs (AOF) plus replication, each with trade-offs in durability and speed. Treat a cache as disposable unless you deliberately configure durability.

text: Conway's law (1967) says that organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure. What is the practical implication for architecture?
options: Every company needs exactly three teams, whatever it is that it builds
Teams should avoid talking to each other, so that their designs stay independent
Architecture is unaffected by people, since only technology decides it
If you want a certain architecture, shape team boundaries and communication to match it
explanation: Four teams building a compiler tend to produce a four-pass compiler. Teams often apply the 'inverse Conway manoeuvre': design team structure to encourage the desired module boundaries.

text: In an 8-bit signed integer using two's complement, what happens when you add 1 to 127?
options: It wraps around to −128
It stays 127
An exception is always thrown
It becomes 128
explanation: The range is −128 to 127. Adding 1 to the largest value overflows into the sign bit and wraps to −128 in languages that wrap silently. Some languages trap or promote to bigger types; know which one you use.

text: What problem did async/await (ES2017) mainly address, building on Promises (ES2015)?
options: It made JavaScript multi-threaded, so that code could run in parallel
It removed the event loop and replaced it with a blocking scheduler
It let asynchronous code be written in a readable, sequential style with try/catch error handling
It compiled JavaScript straight into machine code before running it
explanation: Callbacks led to deeply nested code, Promises flattened chains, and async/await made the flow read top to bottom. It is syntax over Promises; it does not add threads.

text: Which boolean name is least likely to cause bugs and confusion?
options: isNotDisabled
notEnabledFlag
disabledIsFalse
isEnabled
explanation: Positive names avoid double negatives like `if (!isNotDisabled)`. Good names say what a value means in the reader's terms; refactoring a negative flag into a positive one often removes a class of mistakes.

text: Why do many people prefer 'open-weights' over 'open-source' for models whose weights are downloadable?
options: Weights alone usually do not include the training data, code and licence freedoms that open source implies
Weights are physically heavier files than source code, so the name is more accurate
'Open source' is a registered trademark that belongs to a single company
The two terms mean exactly the same thing, so the choice is only style
explanation: Downloadable weights let you run and often fine-tune a model, but licences may restrict use and the data and training code may be unavailable. 'Open-weights' describes what is actually released.

text: How does SentencePiece differ in spirit from tokenizers that first split text on whitespace?
options: It only works for English text, since it relies on the spaces between words
It removes all of the spaces from the text permanently before encoding
It treats the input as a raw character stream (marking spaces as symbols), so it needs no language-specific word splitting
It stores whole sentences as single tokens in a very large vocabulary
explanation: SentencePiece encodes spaces as part of the text, which makes it language-independent and fully reversible. This helps for languages without whitespace-delimited words.

text: Assume an API's rate limit is 200,000 tokens per minute and each request counts its input plus the maximum output you reserve: 3,000 + 500 tokens. About how many requests per minute fit?
explanation: Each request counts 3,500 tokens, and 200,000 ÷ 3,500 ≈ 57. Ignoring the reserved output (200,000 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 66) overestimates. Check how your provider counts limits, and set max output tightly.

text: A chat message contains 20 emoji. How many tokens does it cost?
options: Exactly 20 tokens, because every emoji is always a single token
Exactly 1 token, because the tokenizer groups all emoji together
Zero tokens, since emoji are pictures and not text
Often more than 20, since many emoji are multi-byte and may span several tokens
explanation: Emoji are multi-byte in UTF-8, and a byte-level tokenizer may split rare ones into several tokens, while common ones can be single tokens. Count with the target tokenizer.

text: What does 'tokenizer fertility' measure for a language?
options: How many new words a language creates every year as it grows over time
The average number of tokens needed per word (or per unit of text), where higher values mean less efficient encoding
The number of letters in the alphabet that the language is written with
The speed of the network connection that is used to send the text
explanation: High fertility means more tokens for the same content: higher cost, shorter effective context and sometimes weaker modelling for that language. Comparing fertility across languages exposes tokenizer bias.

text: To benefit from prompt (prefix) caching, how should you order the parts of a prompt?
options: Put the variable user input first and the static instructions at the end
Use a random order every time, so that the cache cannot get stale
Static content such as system instructions, tools and reference documents first, and the changing user input last
Put everything in the middle of the prompt, between two empty lines
explanation: Prefix caching reuses an identical beginning, so stable material must come first and anything that changes per request last. A single changed word near the start invalidates the cached prefix.

text: How should a team choose between AI coding tools for its own codebase?
options: Run a trial on real tasks from your repository and measure test pass rates, time saved and review effort
Pick the tool whose company spends the most on advertising and marketing
Trust the public leaderboards alone, without testing on your own code
Choose randomly, since all of the tools are practically identical
explanation: Public benchmarks may not resemble your code, and some may leak into training data. A small bake-off on your own tasks, with the same acceptance criteria, shows practical value and risks.

text: An assistant can read your email, access private files and send messages. Which combination makes prompt-injection attacks especially dangerous?
options: Only reading public web pages while having no tools and no private data
Only writing poems for the user, with no access to anything private
Access to private data plus exposure to untrusted content plus the ability to send data outside
Using a dark theme in the interface of the assistant
explanation: If a malicious email can instruct the assistant to read secrets and send them out, data leaks. Remove one leg: limit tools, require human approval for external actions, or isolate untrusted content.

text: A marketer wants an AI image of a famous actor appearing to endorse a product. What is the main concern?
options: Using a person's likeness without consent and implying an endorsement raises legal and ethical issues
The image will be too colourful, which is a problem for printed adverts
Actors dislike pixels, so they refuse any image that is generated
None at all, because AI images are always free of any rights
explanation: Likeness, publicity rights and false endorsement rules apply regardless of how an image is made, and platform policies may also prohibit it. Get consent or use original or licensed subjects. This is not legal advice.

text: You must find what changed between two versions of a 60-page contract. Which approach is usually most reliable and economical?
options: Ask the model to compare both of the full documents purely from memory
Read neither of the versions and trust whatever the model returns
Summarise each version separately and then compare the two summaries
Compute a structural diff first, then have the model explain only the changed clauses with their context
explanation: A deterministic diff finds every change exactly and cheaply; the model then interprets the small set of differences. Comparing summaries can miss subtle edits. Legal conclusions still need expert review.

text: An AI search answer about a software package's 'latest version' cites three pages. What should you check?
options: Only the length of the answer, since longer answers are usually more current
The font that the citations are displayed in on the results page
The publication dates of the sources and the package's official release page
Nothing at all, because an AI search answer is always up to date
explanation: Search results can include stale pages, and the tool may merge old and new information. For fast-changing facts, confirm on the official release page or registry.

text: For standard self-attention, roughly how does compute for the attention step scale when you double the sequence length?
options: It stays the same
It roughly quadruples
It doubles
It becomes 10× smaller
explanation: Self-attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows with the square of sequence length. Efficient attention variants and caching change the constants and sometimes the scaling, but long contexts are still expensive.

text: You cannot change the model. Which app-level technique best reduces misses on facts buried in long inputs?
options: Add much more filler text around the facts so that they stand out
Retrieve and re-rank a small set of passages, and ask the model to extract relevant quotes before answering
Remove the question from the prompt so the model reads the facts calmly
Increase the font size of the input so that the model sees it better
explanation: Shrinking and ordering the evidence, then forcing a quote-first step, makes the relevant text explicit before the answer is written. Test the result on your own tasks.

text: A cascade tries a cheap model ($0.20 per 1M tokens) first and escalates to a large one ($3.00 per 1M) when a validator rejects the result, which happens 25% of the time. Assuming equal tokens per call, what is the expected cost per 1M tokens?
explanation: Every request pays the cheap model: $0.20. A quarter also pay the large model: 0.25 × $3.00 = $0.75. Total $0.95, about 32% of always using the large model. The validator's cost and the quality of its judgement must also be counted.

text: Why does serving many concurrent users with very long conversations limit a GPU's throughput?
options: Users must queue up to type their messages one after another
Long text is more colourful, so it takes the GPU longer to draw
Each active request keeps a large KV cache in memory, so memory limits how many can run at once
The tokenizer itself slows down the GPUs whenever a conversation grows
explanation: KV-cache memory grows with sequence length for every active request. When memory is full, fewer requests can be batched together, so throughput falls or requests wait.

text: An inference server runs at 95% utilisation and users see TTFT spikes. What explains it, and what is the remedy?
options: The users are simply impatient, so the spikes can safely be ignored
TTFT depends only on the user's phone and not on the server at all
The model is forgetting words when it is working under heavy load
Queues grow sharply near saturation; keep headroom, add capacity or shed or limit load
explanation: Queueing delays rise steeply as utilisation approaches 100%, even if average capacity looks sufficient. Capacity planning should target headroom for peaks, with autoscaling and admission control.

text: Which Core Web Vitals metric measures how responsive a page is to user interactions throughout the visit?
options: LCP, Largest Contentful Paint
CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift
INP, Interaction to Next Paint
TTFB, Time to First Byte
explanation: INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in 2024 and reflects interaction latency over the page's life. LCP measures loading, CLS measures visual stability and TTFB is server response time.

text: Which is a major cost of sharding a database by user ID?
options: Queries become completely impossible once the data is split into shards
Cross-shard joins and transactions, rebalancing and operational complexity
Indexes stop working on every shard as soon as the data is split
All of the data becomes read-only after it has been sharded
explanation: Sharding spreads data and load, but anything spanning shards (joins, global uniqueness, transactions) becomes hard, hot keys can overload one shard, and resharding is difficult. Exhaust indexing, caching and replicas before sharding.

text: How should you set HTTP caching for fingerprinted assets like app.3f9a1c.js versus the HTML page that references them?
options: Long caching for the HTML page only, and no caching for the assets
No caching for anything at all, so that users always get the newest files
Long max-age (even immutable) for the fingerprinted assets, short or revalidated caching for the HTML
The very same caching setting for both of them, in every case
explanation: A changed file gets a new name, so old URLs can be cached for a year safely. The HTML must refresh quickly so it points to the newest asset names.

text: Traffic arrives in sharp spikes and overwhelms a slow downstream service. Which design helps most, and what does it cost?
options: Put a queue between them with workers and backpressure; it smooths load but adds latency and requires idempotent processing
Remove the downstream service, so that nothing is left to be overwhelmed
Buy a larger monitor so that the operators can watch the spikes better
Retry every failed request immediately until it succeeds, without any delay
explanation: Queues absorb bursts and let workers process at a sustainable rate. In exchange, work completes later, ordering and duplicates need thought, and queue length must be monitored.

text: How would you design a booking flow so that two customers cannot reserve the last seat, even under retries and crashes?
options: Enforce it in the database: an atomic conditional update or a unique constraint on (event, seat), a short-lived hold with expiry, and idempotent confirmation
Use a Redis lock on its own, and assume that it never expires too early
Check the availability in the application code, and insert the booking afterwards
Show a warning to the customers and hope that they agree between themselves
explanation: The database is the source of truth, so the rule belongs where it can be enforced atomically. Holds with expiry release abandoned seats, and idempotency keys make retries safe. A lock held only in application memory or cache can be lost or expire mid-operation.

text: A small clinic wants a website where patients can book appointments. Which parts does it need at the very least?
options: Only a nicely designed frontend, because the bookings can be kept inside each visitor's browser
A frontend for the patients plus a backend with a database that keeps the bookings for everyone
Only a database that patients type their appointments into directly, with no pages or server in between
Only a backend, because patients do not need to see any page or button at all
explanation: Patients need a screen (frontend), and the bookings must be stored and checked in one shared place (backend + database) so two people cannot take the same slot.

text: A school website mostly shows text and photos and must load quickly on cheap phones. Which frontend approach fits best?
options: A heavy single-page app that downloads several megabytes of JavaScript and builds the whole page in the browser before showing anything
A native app that every parent must install from a store before reading the school news
Mostly static or server-rendered pages with very little JavaScript, because content sites load fastest this way
A page made entirely of one huge image so that nothing has to be rendered by the browser
explanation: Content-focused sites gain speed from simple HTML delivered quickly; heavy JavaScript costs time and data on weak phones.

text: A shop stores customers, orders and payments that all refer to each other. Which kind of database fits best, and why?
options: A relational database such as PostgreSQL, because linked data needs relationships, constraints and transactions
A key-value store only, because it is the fastest option and the links between the records can always be handled later in the application code
A plain text file per customer, because files are easy to open and to copy to another computer
A graph visualisation tool, because it draws nice pictures of how customers and orders are connected
explanation: Orders, customers and payments are strongly related and must stay consistent, which is exactly what relational databases with constraints and transactions are built for.

text: A library will have a mobile app and a website that use the same data. How should the backend be organised?
options: Two separate backends with copied rules, one for each client, so that a change for the website can never affect the mobile app
Put all the logic inside the mobile app and let the website copy the results from it
Let each client connect straight to the database with its own password and its own rules
One backend API that both clients call, so the rules live in one place and stay consistent
explanation: A shared API means the business rules are written once; duplicating them in several clients leads to different behaviour and bugs.

text: A team of three students builds a food-ordering app for their university, and the requirements keep changing. Which architecture fits?
options: Ten microservices from the first week, so the app is ready to serve millions of users later
One deployable application with clean internal modules, which is simple to change and to run
Three completely separate apps, one per student, that share data by exchanging files every night
A serverless function for every button, each with its own database and its own deployment
explanation: With a tiny team and shifting requirements, one well-structured application is the cheapest to change; splitting early adds network and deployment costs without benefit.

text: A news homepage is requested thousands of times per minute but changes only every ten minutes. What helps most?
options: Buying a faster monitor for the editors so that they can publish the changes more quickly
Deleting old articles every hour, so that the database always has less data to search
Caching the rendered page for a short time so most visitors get a ready-made copy
Making every visitor wait a random time, so that the requests are spread out evenly
explanation: When data changes rarely but is read constantly, serving a cached copy for a few minutes removes almost all of the database and rendering work.

text: A hospital is building a system for patient records, appointments and prescriptions. Which backend and database foundation is the most sensible, and why?
options: A mature backend framework with a relational database such as PostgreSQL, because the records are linked and need transactions and strict integrity
A schema-less document database for everything, because it is quick to start and fields can change freely without any checks
Shared spreadsheets on a cloud drive, because every member of staff already knows how to use them well
A key-value cache as the main store, because it is the fastest option and data can be rebuilt if it is lost
explanation: Medical data is highly related (patient, visit, prescription) and errors are costly, so ACID transactions, constraints and audit-friendly relational storage are the safest base. Speed of setup or flexibility should not outweigh integrity.

text: The same hospital wants one interface for doctors on desktop computers and another for patients on phones. Which frontend choice is sensible?
options: Write three completely separate codebases in three different languages, so that each one can be perfect for its own group of users
Use one fixed-size desktop page for everyone, because phones can simply zoom in when needed
A component-based web frontend (such as React or Vue) calling the same backend API, with layouts adapted to each user group
Build only a command-line tool, since doctors can learn the commands and patients can ask the staff
explanation: Reusing components and one API keeps behaviour consistent while letting each audience get a suitable layout; separate codebases multiply the maintenance work.

text: A hospital system will start with five developers serving one clinic, but may later cover many hospitals. What should the architecture be at the start?
options: Microservices for every single table in the database, with a network call between them, so that each table can be scaled completely on its own
A distributed system across several cloud regions on day one, in case the clinic grows suddenly
Separate apps for doctors, nurses and patients, with a separate database for every group
A modular monolith with clear boundaries, split into services later only where a real need appears
explanation: Starting modular keeps development fast and cheap and keeps the option to extract a service when scale or team size truly demands it.

text: An external lab sends test results to the hospital system, which is sometimes down for maintenance. How can results be received reliably?
options: Accept them through a queue or an idempotent API with retries, so that no result is lost or processed twice
Ask the lab to resend everything by email whenever the system is back online and the staff finally have some time to process it
Reject every result that arrives while the system is down, because the lab should simply try later
Let the lab write straight into the hospital database, even while maintenance is running on it
explanation: A durable queue or an idempotent endpoint with retries decouples the two systems: results wait safely during downtime and duplicates are harmless.

text: An online pharmacy's product list is read about 500 times more often than it changes. What is the best first improvement?
options: Add a second database server and send every write to both servers at the same instant
Cache the product list and invalidate or refresh it whenever a product is changed
Remove the product images so that each page contains fewer bytes for the database
Ask customers to search less often by hiding the search box on the busiest days
explanation: A read-heavy, rarely changing dataset is the ideal cache candidate; the key detail is invalidation so that customers do not see stale prices or stock.

text: A pharmacy system reduces the stock of a medicine and then charges the customer. If the payment fails, what should happen to the stock change?
options: It stays reduced, because the pharmacist can add the missing boxes back to the shelf tomorrow
It is changed again by a random amount, so that the total stock stays roughly correct
Both steps run in one transaction, so the failed payment rolls the stock change back
It is copied to a backup file and only checked at the end of the month by an accountant
explanation: A transaction makes related changes atomic: either everything succeeds or nothing is applied, which prevents inconsistent stock.

text: A hospital must be able to prove who viewed each patient record and when. Which design decision supports this best?
options: Let every employee use one shared password, so that the system stays simple for the busy staff
Hide the records inside obscure URLs, because only authorised people will know where to find them
Keep the logs on each doctor's own laptop, where they can be deleted when disk space runs out
Individual logins with role-based access, and an append-only audit log written by the backend
explanation: Accountability needs individual identity plus tamper-resistant logging done server-side; shared accounts and client-side logs cannot prove who did what.

text: A booking site is slow every Monday morning when many people book at once. What should the team do first?
options: Measure where the time goes (database, application or network) before deciding what to scale
Immediately buy ten more servers for the site, since traffic spikes are always solved by simply adding more machines to the rack
Block half of the visitors on Mondays so that the other half get a good experience
Rewrite the site in another programming language, because the current one is surely too slow
explanation: Scaling the wrong part wastes money: profiling shows whether the bottleneck is the database, a lock, the app code or the network.

text: A hospital wants to search quickly through millions of free-text doctor notes. What is a sensible addition to its main database?
options: Reading every single note one by one on each search, because the main database is already perfectly adequate for any kind of query
A dedicated search index (such as Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL full-text search) fed from the main database
Moving all notes into a spreadsheet so that staff can use the find command of the spreadsheet program
Deleting notes older than a week, so that the search has fewer documents to look through
explanation: Full-text search needs inverted indexes and ranking; a search index built from the source of truth gives fast results while the main database stays authoritative.

text: A clinic wants its patient app on both Android and iOS, with only a small team. Which approach is a reasonable trade-off?
options: Build two completely separate native apps with two full teams of developers, no matter how small the available budget of the clinic is
Ship only an Android app and tell iOS users to buy a different phone before booking
A cross-platform framework such as Flutter or React Native that shares most code, accepting some platform-specific work
Print the booking forms on paper and photograph them with the phone camera for the staff
explanation: Cross-platform frameworks trade a little native polish for much lower cost and one shared codebase, which suits small teams.

text: A video-consultation feature must keep working even if one data centre fails. Which principle applies?
options: Remove single points of failure with redundancy across zones, health checks and automatic failover
Buy the single most expensive server that is available on the market, since such expensive hardware practically never breaks down
Ask doctors to switch to phone calls whenever the system is not working as expected
Keep one very powerful machine and a printed manual explaining how to restart it
explanation: High availability comes from redundancy and automated failover, not from trusting one machine, however expensive.

text: A hospital must integrate with five external systems (labs, insurance, pharmacies...). How can the core system stay stable when a partner changes its format?
options: Copy each partner's format directly into the core database tables, so that nothing needs translating
Ask all five partners to agree on one new format every time that one of them wants a change
Let the user interface read each partner's raw messages and decide what they mean on its own
An adapter layer per partner that translates its format into the hospital's own internal model
explanation: Isolating each external format behind an adapter confines changes to one place and protects the core domain model.

text: A hospital must store millions of large medical scans. Where should the image files themselves live?
options: As binary columns inside the main patient table, so that every single scan becomes a part of its own record row in the database
In object storage, with only metadata and access rules kept in the database and linked to the files
On the personal computers of the radiologists, so that each scan is close to the person reading it
Inside the application's source code repository, together with the version history of the code
explanation: Large files are cheap and scalable in object storage; the database should keep small, queryable metadata and permissions rather than bulky blobs.

text: A company with 60 developers in 8 teams suffers because deployments block each other, and proposes microservices. What should be checked first?
options: Whether competitors use microservices, because copying them is the safest way to choose
Whether the code can be rewritten from scratch over a single weekend by the best developers
Whether clear domain boundaries and team ownership exist, and the operating cost (monitoring, deployment, data consistency) is affordable
Whether every developer has a second monitor, since microservices need much more screen space
explanation: Microservices pay off when boundaries and ownership are clear and the organisation can afford the added operational complexity; otherwise a modular monolith with better release practices may be enough.

text: Your app crashes only when a user leaves the name field empty. What is the best first step?
options: Rewrite the whole app completely from scratch, so that the problem can never come back again in any form or on any phone
Tell the users never to leave that field empty and move on to the next feature
Reproduce the crash with an empty name and read the error message to find the failing line
Restart the phone many times until the crash happens to disappear by itself
explanation: Debugging starts by reproducing the problem reliably and reading the evidence (the error and its location) before changing anything.

text: You want help writing a polite email to an unhappy customer. How should you use an AI assistant?
options: Describe the situation and the tone, then read and edit its draft before you send it
Paste the customer's name only and send whatever the assistant writes, without reading it
Ask it to decide for you whether the customer deserves an answer at all
Avoid AI completely, because every email written with AI is automatically a mistake
explanation: An assistant is good at drafts, but you stay responsible: give it context, then check facts and tone before sending.

text: A weather app needs a secret API key for a paid weather service. Where should that key be kept?
options: Inside the app's own code, because then every single user can use the weather service without needing any extra setup at all
In a public message on the project's social media page so that the team can find it easily
In the app's text on the screen, so that users can copy it whenever it is needed
On your own backend server, which calls the service for the app, so the key never ships to phones
explanation: Anything inside a shipped app can be extracted; a secret key belongs on a server you control, which acts as a proxy.

text: A website works well with 10 users but crashes with 1,000. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing important, because every website crashes whenever more than a few people use it
Something hits a limit under load (database, memory or a lock), so measure and fix that part
The users are using the website in the wrong way and should be asked to be more patient
The website must be rewritten in a different language, because the current one is too weak
explanation: Failure under load points to a bottleneck; measuring finds which resource saturates, so you fix the real limit instead of guessing.

text: Your support chatbot gives long, vague answers. Which change usually helps most?
options: Tell it its role, who the reader is and the exact format and length that you want
Write the same instruction again in capital letters and add several exclamation marks, so that the model clearly understands how important it is
Ask the users to type shorter questions so that the answers must be shorter too
