Switch the chatbot off at night so that it has enough time to rest and improve
explanation: Clear role, audience, format and length constraints steer a model far better than emphasis or hope.

text: A team must build an admin dashboard with many forms and tables that only staff will use. Which is a reasonable frontend choice?
options: A static page of plain text that has to be reloaded and printed again after every single change that one of the staff members makes
A native desktop program that every employee must install and update by hand each week
A single-page app built with a component framework, because it is interactive and search ranking does not matter
A page made only of images of tables, so that the layout is identical on every screen
explanation: Internal, interactive tools benefit from component-based SPAs; SEO and first-load content, the usual reasons to avoid them, are irrelevant here.

text: A ride app must show driver positions that change every few seconds. Which approach fits best?
options: Ask the rider to refresh the whole page by hand every few seconds whenever they want to see where the driver has moved to
Email the new position to the rider every minute, with a map picture attached to the message
Store the positions in a file and let the rider download that file at the end of the ride
Push updates to the client with WebSockets or server-sent events instead of constant manual reloads
explanation: Frequent server-initiated updates are exactly what push channels such as WebSockets or SSE are designed for.

text: Your AI feature takes 8 seconds to answer and users leave. Which change is most likely to help first?
options: Make the answers twice as long, so that the users have more to read while they wait
Stream the answer as it is generated and send simple requests to a smaller, faster model
Hide the waiting time by removing the loading indicator, so that the page looks finished
Ask the users to buy faster phones, since the delay is caused only by their devices
explanation: Streaming makes the first words appear early, and routing easy requests to smaller models cuts real latency and cost.

text: A banking app moves money from account A to account B. What must the database guarantee?
options: That the debit and the credit happen together or not at all, which is what a transaction provides
That each step is saved to a separate file first, and that the two files are then compared by an accountant at the end of next month
That the customer is shown a success message even if one of the two steps has failed
That the money is moved twice, so that a failure of one copy does not matter at all
explanation: A transaction makes the debit and the credit atomic, so a crash can never leave money removed from one account but not added to the other.

text: A support chatbot mostly answers simple FAQs but sometimes meets a complex complaint. How can its AI costs be controlled?
options: Always use the largest and most expensive model for every single message, to be on the safe side
Reduce the number of customers who are allowed to ask questions during the working day
Send simple questions to a small, cheap model and escalate hard ones to a stronger model
Remove the FAQ answers and make every customer wait for a human to type each reply
explanation: Model routing matches each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, with an escalation path for the hard cases.

text: A hospital wants an AI assistant that answers staff questions from its 500-page policy handbook. Which design is the most sensible?
options: Fine-tune a model once on the handbook and never update it, even when the policies change
Retrieve the relevant handbook passages, give them to the model, and tell it to answer only from them with page references
Let the model answer from its general knowledge, because most hospitals follow the same policies
Paste the whole handbook into every question, even though it is far larger than the model can handle
explanation: Retrieval-augmented answers stay grounded and current: the handbook can change without retraining, and page references let staff verify.

text: An online shop expects ten times its normal traffic on Black Friday. Which preparation is the most sensible?
options: Wait for the day to arrive and then simply see whether the website survives the traffic, since it might turn out to be perfectly fine
Remove all product images the night before, so that the pages become small and plain
Ask the customers to shop on other days by showing a banner at the top of every page
Load-test in advance, cache hot pages and add capacity or autoscaling where the tests show limits
explanation: Load testing reveals real limits before customers do; caching and capacity planning then address them where they matter.

text: A payment partner sometimes sends your webhook the same event twice. How do you avoid processing it twice?
options: Store each event ID and ignore events that were already processed, which makes the handler idempotent
Ask the partner never to send the same event twice and then trust that this promise will always be kept by their systems
Process every event twice on purpose, so that at least one of the two attempts must work
Turn the webhook off, and check the partner's dashboard by hand each morning instead
explanation: Networks deliver at-least-once; an idempotent handler that records processed event IDs makes duplicates harmless.

text: Your AI invoice reader works on test invoices but fails on scanned ones from real customers. What is the best next step?
options: Tell the customers to stop scanning their invoices and to retype every number by hand
Switch to a larger model at once and assume that the problem will disappear automatically
Collect real failing scans into a labelled test set and improve OCR or the prompt measured on it
Delete the failing invoices from the system, so that the accuracy figure looks better
explanation: Real failure cases drive improvement: a labelled test set turns vague complaints into a measurable target.

text: Every UI change in your app keeps breaking the database code. Which structure helps most?
options: Put all of the code in one single file, so that nothing can be located in the wrong place
Separate layers (UI, domain logic, data) with clear interfaces so that changes stay local
Copy the database code into every screen so that each screen can change its own copy freely
Forbid UI changes after the first release, so that the database code can never break again
explanation: Layering with stable interfaces limits the blast radius of a change: UI edits no longer touch storage code.

text: A login rate limiter must allow at most 5 attempts per minute per user across four application servers. Where should the counters live?
options: In each application server's own memory, so that every one of the four servers keeps a separate count for the same user
In the browser's local storage, which the user is able to clear whenever they like
In a text file on one server, which the other three servers read once every night
In a shared fast store such as Redis, with keys that expire, so all servers see the same counters
explanation: Counters must be shared and expire automatically; an in-memory store like Redis provides both with atomic increments.

text: A legal assistant must answer questions over 300 contracts totalling millions of tokens. Which approach is the most practical?
options: Index the contracts, retrieve only the relevant clauses for each question and keep citations
Paste all 300 contracts into a single prompt and hope that the model finds the right clause
Summarise every contract into one sentence and discard the originals to save storage space
Ask the lawyer to read all of the contracts first and then type the answers into the assistant
explanation: Even large windows cannot hold millions of tokens economically; retrieval brings in just the relevant clauses and keeps answers verifiable.

text: A mobile client on a slow network must show a feed. Which API design reduces waiting the most?
options: Return every field of every post, so that the client never needs to ask the server again
Make the client download the entire feed history again every time that the screen opens
Return only the fields the screen needs, paginate the results and let the client cache earlier pages
Send the feed as one large image, so that the phone does not have to parse any data
explanation: On slow links, smaller payloads and fewer round trips matter: field selection, pagination and client caching all cut waiting.

text: A hospital app stores patients' data. Which data should be encrypted?
options: Only the app's logo and colours, since they are the most visible part of the whole system
Data in transit (TLS) and sensitive data at rest, with the keys managed separately from the data
Nothing, because the network of the hospital is private and therefore always completely safe
Only the data of famous patients, since the other records are not interesting to attackers
explanation: Encryption in transit and at rest protects against interception and stolen storage; separating keys from data keeps a leak from exposing everything.

text: Your team lets an AI assistant generate database migrations. Which safeguard matters most?
options: Review each generated migration, test it on a copy of production data and keep a rollback plan
Run every generated migration directly on production, since the AI has seen many migrations
Ask the assistant to confirm that its own migration is correct and accept that confirmation
Skip backups to save time, because AI-written migrations are always reversible by definition
explanation: Migrations can destroy data; AI output must be reviewed and rehearsed on realistic data with a way back, like any other risky change.

text: A chat app stores billions of messages and mostly reads the latest ones of each conversation. What matters most for the schema?
options: Storing each message in its own table, so that every message can be found by its own name
Keeping all messages of all users in one single list, ordered by the first letter of the text
Using no keys at all, so that the database can write each message as fast as possible
Partitioning or keying by conversation and time, so recent messages come from one indexed range read
explanation: Access patterns drive the schema: grouping by conversation and ordering by time makes the common read a cheap, indexed range scan.

text: A hospital's monthly report query joins six tables and slows the live booking system. What is a good fix?
options: Ask the staff to book appointments only when the reports are not running during the day
Run the reports on a read replica or a separate analytics copy so that they do not compete with bookings
Delete the older appointments, so that the report has fewer rows to read each month
Remove the indexes from the booking tables, so that the report can scan them faster
explanation: Heavy analytical reads should be isolated from the transactional workload via a replica or an analytics store.

text: An AI summariser keeps ignoring a key clause that sits in the middle of a 90-page contract. What can you do?
options: Increase the font size of that clause in the original file, so that the model notices it
Run the summariser again and again until it happens to mention the clause by chance
Split the contract into sections, summarise each, and place key clauses at the start and end of the prompt
Tell the model that the clause is very important, and expect that sentence alone to solve it
explanation: Models often attend less to the middle of long inputs; chunking and positioning important text at the edges counters this.

text: A clinic's booking confirmation emails are sometimes sent twice after a server crash. Which pattern prevents this?
options: Make sending idempotent with a unique confirmation ID or an outbox, so a retry never sends a duplicate
Tell the patients to ignore any second email and to delete it as soon as it arrives
Turn off the email feature and ask all patients to call the clinic to confirm bookings
Send every email three times, so that at least one copy surely reaches the patient
explanation: Crash recovery retries work; a unique ID or an outbox lets the system recognise what was already sent and avoid duplicates.

text: During traffic spikes, the workers that consume a message queue fall behind. What helps most?
options: Delete the messages that are older than a few seconds, whether or not they have been processed
Make the producers send the messages more slowly, even when real users are waiting
Restart the queue every hour and hope that the backlog disappears with the restart
Scale out the consumers, apply backpressure and alert on queue length and message age
explanation: Capacity (more consumers), flow control (backpressure) and monitoring (length and age) are the standard tools for queue backlogs.

text: Users complain that the AI feature feels slow, but the average latency looks fine. What should you look at?
options: Only the average, because averages always describe what every user experiences
p95/p99 latency and time to first token per stage, since averages hide slow cases
The number of users who have complained, and ignore every other measurement
The model's size on disk, because it alone determines the speed that users feel
explanation: Averages hide the slow tail that real users notice; percentiles and per-stage timings reveal where the delay occurs.

text: One codebase must serve many hospitals while keeping each hospital's patient data private from the others. Which model fits?
options: Store all patients in one table and rely on the user interface to hide other hospitals' rows
Give every hospital the same shared password so that the data can be moved easily between them
Multi-tenancy with a tenant ID enforced in every query and access check, or separate schemas or databases
Ask each hospital to promise not to look at the data that belongs to the other hospitals
explanation: Isolation must be enforced where the data is accessed (queries, access checks, schemas), not left to the UI or to promises.

text: A hospital's AI assistant must never reveal one patient's data to a user who is not allowed to see it. Which control is essential?
options: Enforce access control in the backend before data reaches the model, never relying on the prompt alone
Write 'do not reveal private data' in the system prompt and trust the model to obey every time
Give the model access to every record, and rely on its good judgement to choose what to show
Hide the assistant's answers in a very small font, so that unauthorised users cannot read them
explanation: Prompts are not security boundaries; data the user may not see must be filtered by deterministic authorisation before the model ever gets it.

text: A hospital must change its database schema with zero downtime. Which migration approach works best?
options: Stop the whole hospital system at night, change everything at once and hope that it all works
Delete the old tables first and rebuild them, since this is the fastest way to reach the new schema
Expand and contract: add new structures, write to both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old ones
Ask the doctors to stop entering new data until the migration has finished completely
explanation: Expand/contract keeps old and new schemas compatible during the transition, so the system stays online and each step is reversible.

text: A post-mortem shows that after a short outage, client retries overloaded the database and prolonged the incident. Which improvement helps most?
options: Make clients retry as fast as possible, so that the service recovers sooner with more traffic
Exponential backoff with jitter, circuit breakers and limits on retries to avoid retry storms
Tell all users to stop using the application for one hour after every incident
Remove the database timeouts, so that requests wait for ever until they eventually finish
explanation: Uncontrolled retries multiply load on a struggling system; backoff with jitter, circuit breakers and retry budgets let it recover.
